rationale: Start with a broad, strong scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall retention window. This gives a first view of whether the mixture is compressed early or spread late, guiding later narrowing of gradient range and time.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing analysis time. Shorten the gradient one step while keeping the same composition window and temperature to test how much run time can be cut before the closest mid-run pair drops below baseline resolution.

The 16 min gradient is very close to the 10 min target and still fully resolved, so one more reduction in gradient time is the most direct route to CRF 1.0 or near it. The critical pair is already the same mid-run pair, making this a clean boundary test before changing other variables.

At 14 min the time term is already zero, so the next gain must come from recovering the single under-resolved pair without pushing the last peak back above 10 min. Narrowing the gradient slightly at the high-organic end should expand selectivity in the crowded mid-region while only modestly increasing the final retention.

The slight reduction of phi1 improved the critical 6/7 pair while keeping the last peak under 10 min, so continue in the same direction by one more step. This should further spread the crowded mid-elution region and may bring the worst pair to full credit without incurring any time penalty.

We now know full resolution is achievable at phi1 0.85 but with a small time penalty, and zero time penalty is achievable at phi1 0.90 with only one slightly weak pair. Shortening tG at phi1 0.90 should pull the last peak back under 10 min while testing whether the stronger slope can still keep the critical pair acceptably close to full resolution.

The limiting issue is selectivity of the 6/7 pair, not gross retention, and temperature is a clean lever to change selectivity while staying near the successful zero-time-penalty method. Dropping T one step should modestly increase retention and may improve that pair enough to reach full resolution while likely keeping the last peak near the 10 min target.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and instead raise phi0 one step to compress early retention while changing the gradient window shape. This may shift the crowded central cluster enough to improve the worst pair without greatly affecting the last peak, which is already comfortably below 10 min at the current best method.

Raising phi0 improved the critical pair while keeping zero time penalty, so now combine that gain with the earlier beneficial reduction in phi1. This should further open the crowded 6/7 region, and there is enough margin below 10 min to absorb some extra retention.

We have reached full score, so the only useful remaining search is to see whether the run can be shortened while preserving full resolution and t_last at or below 10 min. Reducing tG by one step from the current optimum is the cleanest edge test.

Since shortening tG broke the critical pair, return to 14 min and test whether a slightly narrower upper range can maintain full resolution while nudging selectivity and possibly improving margin around the optimum. This checks whether injection 9 is a true plateau or a narrow point optimum.

The optimum appears to sit on a time/selectivity knife-edge near phi1 0.85, so test whether raising phi0 one more step can preserve or improve the critical mid-run spacing while pulling the last peak slightly earlier. This is a targeted attempt to create a more robust full-resolution method around the current best point.

This new full-score method has better time margin than injection 9, so it is the best starting point for another shortening test. Reducing tG by one step checks whether the added robustness from higher phi0 is enough to keep the critical pair resolved while further cutting run time.

Shortening to 12 min again broke the same critical pair, so stay at 14 min and probe whether a slightly lower phi1 can give more selectivity margin while still keeping the last peak under 10 min. With injection 12 at 9.59 min, there is room for a modest retention increase.

Increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved full score and improved time margin, so one more step upward is the most logical test for an even more robust optimum. This may keep the critical pair resolved while pulling the last peak earlier than the current best methods.

At phi0 0.20 the critical pair weakened, so the sweet spot for phi0 appears to be near 0.15. Testing phi0 0.15 with a slightly higher phi1 maps the other side of the current optimum and checks whether full score can be maintained with a different balance of selectivity and retention.

The best methods all sit at 40 C, but we have not tested whether a higher temperature can preserve full resolution while giving more room below the 10 min limit. A one-step increase from the known optimum is a focused robustness check that could reveal a second full-score plateau.

Temperature changes were strongly detrimental, and the 12 min test showed the optimum loses resolution as the slope steepens. A 16 min run at the known good composition window checks whether extra gradient time provides a wider robustness margin around the critical pair while likely keeping full resolution.

Two full-score methods have been found at 40 C, and phi0 0.15 gave the best time margin; testing the same composition at 45 C completes the local robustness map around that optimum. This checks whether the higher-phi0 optimum responds differently to temperature than the phi0 0.10 case.

Higher temperature clearly damages the key selectivity, so one final local temperature probe on the low side will complete the map around the best composition. If 35 C also worsens the 6/7 pair, we confirm 40 C as the unique optimum and can stop searching temperature.

With 40 C confirmed best and 14 min established as the only full-resolution time at the main optima, use a remaining injection to test whether the stronger selectivity at lower phi1 can compensate for a shorter 12 min gradient. This is the best remaining chance to find a faster full-score method than the existing 14 min solutions.

The 12 min run at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.80 came surprisingly close, and phi0 0.15 was the more robust setting at 14 min. Combining those two favorable trends is the strongest remaining shot at finding a shorter fully resolved method.

The 12 min methods at phi1 0.80 consistently miss full resolution only slightly, so one last composition-window shift is worth testing. Raising phi0 may alter the crowded mid-gradient selectivity enough to push the 6/7 pair over 1.5 while the last peak should remain safely under 10 min.

Across the 12 min runs, increasing phi0 did not rescue the critical pair, so test the opposite extreme of phi0 at the same phi1 to complete the trend and check for a nonmonotonic selectivity effect. This is one of the few untried 12 min variants that could still conceivably push the 6/7 pair over 1.5.

For the last shot at a faster full-score method, probe whether the near-miss 12 min, phi0 0.10/phi1 0.90 condition can gain selectivity from lower temperature enough to offset its weak 6/7 pair. This specific combination has not been tested, and despite temperature risks it is one of the few remaining plausible ways to rescue a 12 min method.
